claims.text: Mechanical-property differences among equiatomic Cr-Mn-Fe-Co-Ni and its quaternary and ternary subsets are governed by variations in local chemical short-range order and lattice distortion.
Differences in constituent atomic sizes and electronegativities induce differences in short-range order and lattice distortion.
Short-range order and lattice distortion alter dislocation mobility and deformation mechanisms.
Consistent thermomechanical processing will produce similarly homogenized microstructures across the single-phase FCC quinary, quaternary, and ternary alloys.
The degree of chemical short-range order varies with the number and identity of the alloying elements.
The magnitude of local lattice distortion varies with the number and identity of the alloying elements.
Local lattice distortions create heterogeneous strain fields that can hinder or promote dislocation motion.
Larger atomic-size and electronegativity differences increase lattice distortion.
Increased lattice distortion raises yield strength by impeding dislocation mobility.
Increased lattice distortion can reduce ductility.
Reduced lattice distortion permits easier dislocation motion, producing lower strength and greater ductility.
Lattice distortion and short-range order can affect the onset of deformation twinning.
Relative to the equiatomic quinary baseline, quaternary and ternary alloys having lower lattice distortion will exhibit lower yield strength and greater ductility.
Compositions that enhance local short-range order may exhibit greater strength.
Compositions that enhance local short-range order may show earlier twinning under high-strain-rate deformation.
Equiatomic Cr-Mn-Fe-Co-Ni has balanced lattice distortion and intermediate short-range order and therefore represents a midpoint in mechanical behavior.

The proposed relationships apply when the alloys remain single-phase FCC, receive similar thermomechanical processing, contain nanoscale heterogeneities, and deform primarily by dislocation activity rather than phase transformation.
Solute drag may also contribute to the observed mechanical-property differences.
